lessons.title: मित्रम् (mitram) — "friend," and the god of the given word
lessons.gloss: friend — the word behind a covenant-god's name, naming a person while itself being neuter

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page

segments.text: Say "food," and its gender. (Annam; neuter.) The last three words named things you would ask for. This one names someone you would introduce.

utterances: Sanskrit: मित्रम्. sound: mitram. meaning: friend.
Sanskrit: मित्रम् मम. sound: mitram mama. meaning: my friend.

segments.text: मि is mi, a short vowel sign under म. त्र stacks त ta under र ra, said as one push, tra. म् closes it, neuter again: mi-tra-m.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — the god of the given word

segments.text: मित्रम् (mitram) comes from Proto-Indo-Iranian mitras, "that which causes binding" — a promise, a pact, a bond between two people. The same word names Mithra, the Avestan and Zoroastrian god of covenant and contract: a friendship, at the root, is a kind of oath.
It travelled east with almost no change at all: Hindi and Marathi मित्र, Gujarati mitra, all तत्सम, lifted straight out of Sanskrit rather than worn down the way पानीयम् became pānī.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: a person, grammatically neuter

segments.text: Here is the proof that gender is not about meaning. मित्रम् (mitram) names a person, and Sanskrit still marks it neuter — the same -म् you have now seen on water, milk, and food. A noun's gender is a fact about the word, inherited with its shape, not a fact about who or what it points to.

segments.instruction: the god it shares a name with — Mithra

segments.text: What does the root behind मित्रम् mean, and what god shares it? ("To bind"; Mithra, the covenant god.) Is मित्र in Hindi तत्सम or तद्भव? (तत्सम.) What gender is mitram, and why is that surprising? (Neuter — it names a person, but gender tracks the word's class, not the person.)

lessons.title: कुटुम्बम् (kuṭumbam) — "family," a word that made a round trip
lessons.gloss: family, household — a word Sanskrit itself borrowed, before other languages borrowed it back

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Say "friend," and its gender. (Mitram; neuter.) One person's name, now the group everyone belongs to.

utterances: Sanskrit: कुटुम्बम्. sound: kuṭumbam. meaning: family, household.
Sanskrit: मम कुटुम्बम्. sound: mama kuṭumbam. meaning: my family.

segments.text: कु is ku, a short-u sign under क. टु repeats it under the curled-back ट, the retroflex t you first met in संस्कृत's neighbours. म्ब stacks ब ba under a silent म्, and a final म् closes it: ku-ṭu-mba-m.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — a word that made a round trip

segments.text: Every etymology so far in this chapter has run from Sanskrit outward. This one runs the other way first. कुटुम्बम् (kuṭumbam) is a loanword into Sanskrit from a Dravidian language, compared to Tamil kuṭimai, "family, lineage, allegiance," itself built on kuṭi, "a hut, a settlement." A family, on this account, is literally those who share one roof.

From Sanskrit the finished word travelled onward as a formal, learned तत्सम — Hindi कुटुंब and Bengali kuṭumbo — and then made a full circle: Kannada, Telugu and Tamil today all hold this same Sanskrit-shaped form, borrowed back into languages that, on one account, lent Sanskrit the word in the first place.

segments.instruction: which family lent Sanskrit the word — Dravidian
segments.source: [YOU SAY: which family lent Sanskrit the word — Dravidian]

segments.instruction: the languages that later borrowed it back — Kannada, Telugu, Tamil
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the languages that later borrowed it back — Kannada, Telugu, Tamil]

segments.text: Which direction did कुटुम्बम् (kuṭumbam) travel first — into Sanskrit, or out of it? (Into it — a Dravidian loanword.) What Tamil word is it compared to, and what does it literally build on? (kuṭimai, "family, lineage," on kuṭi, "a hut.") Which languages later borrowed the Sanskrit-shaped form back? (Kannada, Telugu, Tamil.)

lessons.title: भ्राता (bhrātā) — "brother," the same word, worn two ways
lessons.gloss: brother — unbroken from Sanskrit to English, worn down two different ways

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Say "family" and "friend." (Kuṭumbam, mitram.) Now for the first person inside that family — and the plainest cousin in this book yet.

utterances: Sanskrit: भ्राता. sound: bhrātā. meaning: brother.
Sanskrit: मम भ्राता. sound: mama bhrātā. meaning: my brother.

segments.text: Masculine — the first noun this chapter has not ended in -म्.
भ्रा stacks र ra under भ bha, one push, then the long-ā: bhrā. ता closes it, ta plus long-ā again: bhrā-tā.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — the same word, worn two ways

segments.text: भ्राता (bhrātā) is PIE bhrāter-, and the descent is about as unbroken as this family gets: English brother, Latin frāter, Greek phrātēr are not relatives of भ्राता (bhrātā) — they are भ्राता (bhrātā), six thousand years and three different roads later.

One of those roads runs straight through the daughter languages. भ्राता (bhrātā) wore down through Prakrit bhāi into Bengali bhāi and Gujarati bhāī, both तद्भव — the same word again, just worn smooth by everyday speech rather than lifted whole like मित्र.

Grammatically, भ्राता (bhrātā) is a fossil of its own: an old kinship word built on the stem भ्रातृ (bhrātṛ), whose nominative singular lengthens the final vowel to -आ instead of following the plain patterns you have seen so far.

segments.instruction: its English, Latin, and Greek selves — brother, frāter, phrātēr
segments.source: [YOU SAY: its English, Latin, and Greek selves — brother, frāter, phrātēr]

segments.text: Is English brother a cousin of भ्राता (bhrātā), or the same word? (The same word, unbroken from PIE.) Which two daughter languages wore it down to bhāi? (Bengali, Gujarati.) What gender is भ्राता (bhrātā), unlike every noun before it this chapter? (Masculine.)

lessons.title: भगिनी (bhaginī) — "sister," one with a share
lessons.gloss: sister — not built on English "sister"'s root at all, but on "one with a share"

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Say "brother," and name the English word it is not a cousin of but literally is. (Bhrātā; brother.) The matching word does not tell the same story.

utterances: Sanskrit: भगिनी. sound: bhaginī. meaning: sister.
Sanskrit: मम भगिनी. sound: mama bhaginī. meaning: my sister.

segments.text: Feminine — marked by the -ई you can hear at the end.
भ is bha. गि is ग ga under a short-i sign. नी closes it, न under the long-ī sign — the same feminine ending you will meet again this book: bha-gi-nī.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — one with a share

segments.text: Here the pattern breaks. भगिनी (bhaginī) is built on भग (bhaga), "a share, good fortune," plus the feminine suffix -इनी: literally, "one with a share."

Sanskrit's actual cousin of English sister is a different word, स्वसृ (svasṛ), from the same PIE root as bhrātā's. It is real, attested in the old texts — but it did not become the everyday word. भगिनी (bhaginī) did, and भगिनी (bhaginī) is what wore down eastward: Bengali bon and Gujarati bahen, both तद्भव, both built on भग, not स्वसृ.

So the honest connection to draw for "sister" is not the one nearest to English. Brother and sister do not travel the same road here — one is the same word worn down; the other took a different word entirely and left the matching one behind.

Mitram, kuṭumbam, bhrātā, bhaginī — a friend, a family, a brother, a sister. One borrowed into Sanskrit and then borrowed back out; two travelled in lockstep with their English match; one quietly swapped words along the way.

segments.text: What does भगिनी literally mean? ("One with a share.") What is the actual PIE cousin of English sister, and why is it not the word we learned? (स्वसृ — attested, but never the living word.) Which two daughter languages descend from भगिनी instead? (Bengali, Gujarati.) Name this chapter's four people. (Mitram, kuṭumbam, bhrātā, bhaginī.)

lessons.title: आ (ā) — one character, met inside words you already say
lessons.gloss: the single character आ — recognised inside words you already say

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: आ and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Before the new one: अ — what does it do?
One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
आ — ā.
It is an independent vowel — the shape the vowel ā takes when a word begins with it, rather than the sign it becomes inside a word.
What it is made of:
the joined upper-and-lower left body of अ.
a middle shoulder.
an inner vertical stem.
a trailing vertical stem.
the top shirorekhā.
You already say these, and every one of them has आ (ā) somewhere inside it:
आम् / न ām / na — yes / no (ām / na).
आनन्दः ānandaḥ — joy — and "meeting you is a joy.
आगच्छति āgacchati — he, she, or it comes.
1. curve around the upper bowl, then continue down and around the lower bowl without lifting.
2. lift and sweep the middle shoulder right.
3. lift and draw the inner stem top-to-bottom.
4. lift and draw the trailing stem top-to-bottom.
5. lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right.
Pen lifts: 4. The pen comes up 4 times and no more.
Verified modern printed teaching form; other Devanagari traditions split the shared अ body into more strokes.

This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Saurmandal, ‘Devanagari आ (ā) stroke order.svg’, frames 1–5, Wikimedia Commons, 5 August 2023.

lessons.title: र — one character, met inside words you already say
lessons.gloss: the single character र — recognised inside words you already say

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: र and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Before the new one: ◌ि — what does it do?
One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
र — ra.
It is a consonant, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an a already in it. So it is not r, it is ra.
What it is made of:
a top-to-bottom stem curling clockwise around the lower loop.
a diagonal tail.
the top shirorekhā.
You already say these, and every one of them has र (ra) somewhere inside it:
नमस्कारः namaskāraḥ — hello (lit. "the making of a bow") (namaskāraḥ).
पुनर्दर्शनाय punardarśanāya — until we meet again (lit. "for seeing again").
करोमि karomi — I do, I make (कार्यं करोमि, "I work").
एक द्व त्रि चतुर् पञ्च eka dva tri catur pañca — one to five.
1. start at the headline junction, descend the stem, and curl left and clockwise around the lower loop to the tail junction.
2. lift at that junction and draw the diagonal tail down-right.
3. lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right.
Pen lifts: 2. The pen comes up 2 times and no more.
Verified three-stroke teaching form; another animated learner source joins the loop and diagonal tail.

This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Opiaterein, ‘Deva-र (ra)-order.gif’, strokes 1–3, Wikimedia Commons, 10 May 2009.
